title: Wandering for Christ
hookLine: Irish monks set out in boats without oars, going where God led

lines: A BOAT OF HIDES, NO OARS.
FOR THE LOVE OF GOD, THEY CARED NOT WHERE.
cards: Three men wash up on the coast of Cornwall in a little boat made of hides. The boat has no oars. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, an old English record, tells it plainly.
They had slipped away from Ireland because they wanted to be on pilgrimage for the love of God, and they did not care where. They took food for about a week and let the sea carry them.
Then they were brought before King Alfred, who must have had questions. Nobody had steered. That was the whole point.
Irish Christians had a Latin word for setting out like this: peregrinatio. Wandering for Christ.

teach.b: In everyday Latin, peregrinatio meant living abroad, being the foreigner in town. Irish Christians gave it a sharper edge: leaving home on purpose, as an offering to God. Not a trip with a ticket back.
An exile you chose. Some looked back to Abraham.

teach.h: GET THEE OUT OF THY COUNTRY.
teach.b: In Genesis, God says to him: "Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee." No map, just a promise.
Hebrews says "he went out, not knowing whither he went," and a few verses on calls the people of faith "strangers and pilgrims on the earth." Some Irish monks took that at its word.
Columba, met back on day seven hundred eighty-eight, left Ireland and settled on Iona; his biographer Adomnán says he sailed away wishing to be a pilgrim for Christ.
Others, the stories say, pushed out with no plan and let the wind and the current choose the shore. A boat without oars sounds reckless.
To them it was trust you could see. Where they landed, the stories go on, they prayed, and some built a small community and stayed for life. Christians read this old practice in more than one way.
Some hear a call that came to a few, and still comes, to leave everything. Some walk long pilgrim roads for a season.
And some hear a picture of the inner life: holding plans loosely, and saying yes to the place where you've been set down.

how: Some Christians today go on walking pilgrimages, including to old Celtic sites such as Iona; others take the Irish idea of peregrinatio inwardly, as a way of holding their plans loosely and trusting God to lead.

a Latin hymn sung by sailors before a long sea voyage

games.q: you're one of the three in the chronicle, standing by a small boat of hides. there are no oars. what do you do?
o: wait for calmer weather and a crew.
push off and let God and the wind decide.
row along the coast where it's safe.
games.why: they pushed off with food for about a week and came ashore in Cornwall. they wanted to be on pilgrimage for the love of God, the chronicle says, and did not care where.

practice: Bring today's plan to mind and look for one small gap you could leave open: a different street home, a bench you've never sat on, a door you always walk past, without picking where it leads.
Notice what happens in you as you loosen your grip on the oars, even a little. If you pray, hold the open space before God, the way Abraham set out.

wordCard.voice: Peregrinatio. Latin for living abroad; for the Irish saints, leaving home for the love of God and going where they were led.

orig.note: Latin: living abroad, a stay far from home; to the Irish saints, an exile chosen for Christ.

carryVoice: Your line: where the wind takes. Plans held loosely leave room for a shore nobody chose. Until tomorrow.
